title: Towards Understanding the Role of Sharpness-Aware Minimization Algorithms for Out-of-Distribution Generalization
main_claims: SAM outperforms Adam by 4.76% on average on zero-shot OOD generalization across four benchmarks, with the strongest SAM variants (FisherSAM, FriendlySAM) achieving up to 8.01% improvement.
SAM also improves gradual domain adaptation (GDA) performance by 0.82% on average, with stronger variants achieving 1.52% improvement.
The theoretical OOD generalization bound derived for SAM is asymptotically no better than prior self-training bounds, highlighting a gap between theoretical justification and empirical performance.
methodology: Eight SAM variants are compared on four benchmark datasets (Color MNIST, Rotated MNIST, Cover Type, Portraits) in zero-shot OOD and gradual domain adaptation settings. CNN and MLP architectures are trained with Adam baseline and all SAM variants; hyperparameters are grid-searched over ρ ∈{0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2}. Theoretical bounds extending Foret et al.'s PAC-Bayes bound to OOD and GDA settings are also derived.
key_results: SAM outperforms Adam by 4.76% average on zero-shot OOD (Table 2); FriendlySAM achieves +8.01%.
SAM outperforms Adam by 0.82% average on GDA; FriendlySAM achieves +1.52%.
The derived OOD generalization bound for SAM is of the same asymptotic rate as prior GDA bounds, highlighting that theory does not fully explain SAM's empirical OOD gains.
limitations: Benchmarks are limited to relatively simple OOD shifts (color/rotation of MNIST, Cover Type, Portraits); not evaluated on CIFAR-C or ImageNet-C.
Theoretical bounds are loose and asymptotically equivalent to non-SAM baselines, leaving the empirical advantage unexplained.
Experiments use modest architectures (4-layer CNN, 3-layer MLP) rather than ResNets.
relevance_to_rq: Directly relevant: this paper empirically shows SAM improves zero-shot OOD generalization and acknowledges the gap between flatness theory and empirical gains, citing work showing low sharpness alone does not account for all SAM benefits. This supports the RQ's premise and motivates the representation-stability alternative explanation.

key_quotes.text: the original SAM outperforms the Adam baseline by 4.76% and the strongest SAM variants outperform the Adam baseline by 8.01% on average.
key_quotes.context: Main zero-shot OOD result showing SAM's empirical advantage

key_quotes.text: This highlights a further disconnection between the theoretical justification for SAM versus its empirical performance, as noted in Wen et al. (2023), which found that low sharpness alone does not account for all of SAM's generalization benefits.
key_quotes.context: Acknowledgement that flatness alone is insufficient to explain SAM's OOD gains

key_quotes.text: SAM has been found to lead to lower rank features with fewer active ReLU units, to enhance feature quality by selecting more balanced features, to enhance robustness to label noise through implicitly regularizing the model Jacobian
key_quotes.context: Survey of SAM's implicit biases beyond flatness
